question: Can a grappled creature still attack and cast spells?
ruling: The grappled condition sets a creature's speed to 0 and denies it any bonus to its speed, and that is all it does. It does not incapacitate the creature or limit its actions, so a grappled creature can still take the Attack action or cast a spell. Only its movement is stopped.

question: Can I drag the creature I'm grappling when I move?
verdict: yes, at half speed unless it is two or more sizes smaller
ruling: When you move, you can drag or carry the creature you are grappling, but your speed is halved, unless the creature is two or more sizes smaller than you. So you can drag it, and you move at half speed unless it is at least two sizes smaller than you.

question: Can the grappled creature escape with Acrobatics instead of Athletics?
ruling: A grappled creature can use its action to escape by succeeding on a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check contested by the grappler's Strength (Athletics) check. Acrobatics is one of the two named options, so the grappled creature can use it.

question: Can I grapple a creature two sizes larger than me?
ruling: The target of a grapple must be no more than one size larger than you. A creature two sizes larger is outside that limit, so you can't grapple it.

question: Do attackers get advantage against a grappled creature?
ruling: The grappled condition sets a creature's speed to 0 and denies it any bonus to its speed. It says nothing about attack rolls against the creature. The restrained condition is the one that gives attackers advantage, and being grappled is not being restrained, so attackers get no advantage from the grapple.

question: Can I hold a grapple with one hand and still attack with a two-handed weapon?
ruling: Reading A: yes. The grapple rule asks for a free hand only to seize the target, and the grappled condition lists what ends it: the grappler being incapacitated, or the grappled creature being moved out of reach. Putting a second hand on a weapon is neither, so the grapple holds while you attack with the weapon in both hands. Reading B: no. You seize the target using a free hand, and a grapple held is a hand still holding the creature. The two-handed property requires two hands when you attack with the weapon, and the hand holding the grapple is not free to be one of them, so attacking with it means releasing the grapple, which you can do whenever you like. Why the text does not settle it: the free hand is named for the attempt to seize, not for holding on, and the two-handed property asks for two hands at the attack without saying whether a hand holding a grapple can be one.

question: I shove a creature I'm grappling prone. Can it stand up?
ruling: Standing up costs movement equal to half your speed, and you can't stand up if your speed is 0. A grappled creature's speed becomes 0. While the grapple lasts, the prone creature has no movement to spend, so it can't stand up; it has to escape the grapple first.

question: Does the Dodge action still work while I'm grappled?
ruling: Dodge's benefit is lost if you are incapacitated or if your speed drops to 0. A grappled creature's speed becomes 0, and it can't benefit from any bonus to its speed. While you are grappled your speed is 0, so you can take the Dodge action but gain nothing from it: attacks against you don't have disadvantage and your Dexterity saving throws don't have advantage.

question: If the creature grappling me is knocked prone, does the grapple end?
ruling: A grapple ends only if the grappler is incapacitated or the grappled creature is moved out of the grappler's reach. The prone condition does not make the grappler incapacitated, and being knocked prone moves neither creature, so the grappled creature stays within reach and the grapple continues.

question: Can I grapple and shove in the same Attack action?
verdict: yes, if the Attack action gives you more than one attack
ruling: A grapple and a shove are each a special melee attack made with the Attack action, and if you can make multiple attacks with that action, each replaces one of them. The Attack action makes one attack unless a feature such as Extra Attack grants more. With two or more attacks, one can be a grapple and another a shove; with one attack, you can do only one of them.

question: Do enemies know where an invisible creature is?
ruling: Reading A: enemies know where an invisible creature is until it hides. An invisible creature can always try to hide, and for the purpose of hiding it is heavily obscured, which makes hiding a separate step that invisibility makes possible rather than one it performs. The hiding rules add that an invisible creature has to stay quiet and that signs of its passage might be noticed, which matters only if hiding is what conceals it. Reading B: enemies don't know where it is unless it gives itself away. An invisible creature is impossible to see, and its location can be detected by any noise it makes or any tracks it leaves; naming how the location can be detected implies it is otherwise unknown. Attacking an unseen target allows for guessing its location, which fits a creature that can't be seen and hasn't been heard. Why the text does not settle it: the invisible condition says how a location can be found, and the hiding rules say how it can be concealed, but neither says whether an invisible creature that has not hidden starts out located or unlocated.

question: An invisible attacker attacks an invisible target. What is rolled?
ruling: An invisible creature's attack rolls have advantage, and attack rolls against an invisible creature have disadvantage. Here the attacker is invisible, which grants advantage, and the target is invisible, which imposes disadvantage. A roll with both advantage and disadvantage has neither, so one d20 is rolled.

question: If I attack from hiding and miss, am I revealed?
ruling: If you are hidden, both unseen and unheard, when you make an attack, you give away your location when the attack hits or misses. A miss is named alongside a hit, so the attack reveals your location either way.

question: Can I hide mid-combat while the enemy is distracted, without cover?
ruling: Reading A: no. You can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly, and in combat most creatures stay alert for signs of danger all around. The rule about a distracted creature lets you stay hidden as you approach it, which assumes you were already hidden; it does not let you become hidden in plain view. Reading B: yes, if the GM allows it. The GM decides when circumstances are appropriate for hiding, and a creature whose attention is elsewhere is not seeing you clearly, so distraction can be the circumstance. Why the text does not settle it: seeing clearly is not defined, so the text does not say whether it turns only on what blocks sight or also on where a creature's attention is.

question: Can I hide behind an ally?
ruling: Reading A: yes, if the ally blocks the enemy's view of you. The GM decides when circumstances are appropriate for hiding, and the cover rules name creatures among the obstacles that can come between you and an attacker, so an ally standing between you and an enemy can be the circumstance that lets you hide. Reading B: no. You can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly, and cover is defined by how hard a target is to harm, not by whether it can be seen. A creature typically gives half cover, which blocks at least half of your body and leaves the rest in view. Why the text does not settle it: the hiding rule turns on being seen clearly and the cover rule turns on being harder to hit, and no rule says whether a creature in the way blocks sight. The answer is left to the GM's call on the circumstances.

question: Can I hide in an area that is only lightly obscured?
ruling: Reading A: yes. You can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly, and a lightly obscured area, such as dim light or patchy fog, gives creatures disadvantage on Perception checks that rely on sight. A creature that has trouble seeing into the area is not seeing you clearly, and the hiding rules name light and heavy obscurement as the main factor in finding a hidden creature. Reading B: no. Light obscurement only penalizes Perception checks; creatures still see into the area. It is heavy obscurement that blocks vision entirely, so only that, or something else that blocks sight, keeps you from being seen clearly. Why the text does not settle it: seeing clearly is not tied to either degree of obscurement, so the text does not say which one is enough to hide.

question: Two creatures without darkvision fight in magical darkness. What is rolled?
ruling: Darkness is heavily obscured, and a creature trying to see something in a heavily obscured area effectively suffers from the blinded condition. When you attack a target you can't see, you have disadvantage, and when a creature can't see you, you have advantage on attack rolls against it. Neither creature can see the other, so each attack has both advantage and disadvantage, which cancel: one d20 is rolled.

question: Does darkvision let me see an invisible creature?
ruling: An invisible creature is impossible to see without the aid of magic or a special sense. Darkvision lets a creature see in darkness as if it were dim light, and that is all it changes; it says nothing about invisible creatures. Truesight is the sense that names seeing invisible creatures. Darkvision treats darkness, not invisibility, so it does not reveal an invisible creature.

question: Does the Search action find an invisible creature?
verdict: it can find the creature's location, not make it visible
ruling: The Search action devotes your attention to finding something, with a Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation) check as the GM decides. An invisible creature is impossible to see without magic or a special sense, but its location can be detected by any noise it makes or any tracks it leaves; if it is hiding, your Perception check is contested by its Stealth check. A successful Search can find where the creature is through those signs, but it does not let you see it.

question: Does a hidden creature stay hidden when it moves?
verdict: yes, while it stays out of clear sight and quiet
ruling: A hiding creature's Stealth check stands until it is discovered or stops hiding, and it gives away its position if it makes noise. You can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly, and a creature that comes out of hiding and approaches an enemy is usually seen. Moving is not itself named as ending the hide, so a creature that moves while staying out of clear sight and making no noise stays hidden; moving into clear view, or making noise, reveals it.

question: I have advantage from two sources and disadvantage from one. What is rolled?
ruling: If circumstances cause a roll to have both advantage and disadvantage, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one d20. This is true even if multiple circumstances impose disadvantage and only one grants advantage or vice versa. Two sources of advantage and one of disadvantage still give the roll both, so they cancel and you roll one d20.

question: I make a ranged attack against a prone target from 5 feet. What is rolled?
ruling: An attack roll against a prone creature has advantage if the attacker is within 5 feet of it. A ranged attack has disadvantage if you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature who can see you and isn't incapacitated, and being prone does not incapacitate the target. At 5 feet the attack has both advantage and disadvantage, which cancel, so one d20 is rolled.

question: A ranged attack hits an unconscious creature from 5 feet. Is it a critical hit?
ruling: Any attack that hits an unconscious creature is a critical hit if the attacker is within 5 feet of it. The rule says any attack, not any melee attack, and 5 feet is within 5 feet, so the ranged hit is a critical. The close-range penalty does not apply either: it needs a hostile creature that isn't incapacitated, and an unconscious creature is incapacitated.

question: Attacking a paralyzed creature from 30 feet: do I have advantage, and is a hit a critical?
ruling: Attack rolls against a paralyzed creature have advantage, with no limit on distance. Any attack that hits it is a critical hit only if the attacker is within 5 feet of it. At 30 feet you have advantage, but 30 feet is beyond 5 feet, so a hit is an ordinary hit, not a critical.

question: Does a critical hit double the flat damage modifiers?
ruling: On a critical hit you roll all of the attack's damage dice twice and add them together, then add any relevant modifiers as normal. Only the dice are doubled; the modifiers are added once, so a dagger critical is 2d4 plus the ability modifier, not twice the modifier.

question: Does a natural 20 on an ability check always succeed?
ruling: The rule that a 20 succeeds regardless of modifiers is written for the d20 roll for an attack. An ability check succeeds by meeting the DC the GM sets for the task, and no rule gives a 20 on an ability check an automatic success. A natural 20 on a check succeeds only if the total meets the DC.

question: Does a natural 1 on a saving throw always fail?
ruling: The rule that a 1 misses regardless of modifiers is written for the d20 roll for an attack. A saving throw is a d20 plus the ability modifier against a DC set by the effect, and no rule makes a 1 on a save an automatic failure. A natural 1 on a save fails only if the total falls short of the DC.

question: I take damage from two attacks. How many concentration saves do I make?
ruling: Whenever you take damage while concentrating, you make a Constitution saving throw, with a DC of 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher. If you take damage from multiple sources, you make a separate saving throw for each source of damage. Two attacks are two sources, so you make two saves, each with its DC set by that attack's damage.

question: Does being knocked unconscious end concentration?
ruling: You lose concentration on a spell if you are incapacitated. An unconscious creature is incapacitated, so being knocked unconscious ends concentration.

question: Can I cast a spell that doesn't need concentration while concentrating on another?
ruling: Casting another spell breaks concentration only if that spell also requires concentration. A spell that doesn't require concentration is not on the list of things that break it, so you can cast it and keep concentrating on the first.

question: I cast a spell as a bonus action. Can I cast a cantrip with my action?
verdict: yes, if the cantrip's casting time is 1 action
ruling: After casting a spell with a bonus action, you can't cast another spell during the same turn, except for a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. A cantrip cast with your action is that exception, so it is allowed as long as its casting time is 1 action.

question: On a turn I cast a bonus-action spell, can I cast a leveled spell as a reaction?
verdict: no, cantrips with 1 action casting time only
ruling: If you cast a spell with a bonus action, you can't cast another spell during the same turn, except for a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. A spell cast as a reaction on that same turn is another spell during the same turn, and a leveled spell is not a cantrip, so it can't be cast. The limit holds for that turn only: on another creature's turn, the reaction spell is allowed.

question: Does a spell I Ready count against the bonus-action spell rule when I release it?
verdict: it counts on the turn you ready it, not when you release it
ruling: When you ready a spell, you cast it as normal on your turn and hold its energy, then release it with your reaction when the trigger occurs. After a bonus-action spell, you can't cast another spell during the same turn except a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. The casting happens on the turn you take the Ready action, so a bonus-action spell that turn allows readying only such a cantrip; releasing the spell later is not a casting and does not count again.

question: I Ready a spell and the trigger never comes. Is the spell slot spent?
ruling: When you ready a spell, you cast it as normal and hold its energy, and when a character casts a spell, they expend a slot of that spell's level or higher. The slot is spent at the casting, on your turn. The Ready action only lasts until the start of your next turn, so if the trigger never comes, the held spell is lost and the slot stays spent.

question: Two casters put the same spell on me. Do both apply?
ruling: The effects of the same spell cast multiple times don't combine; the most potent effect from those castings applies while their durations overlap. Two castings of the same spell on you are that case, so only the stronger one applies; if two clerics cast bless on you, you roll one bonus die, not two.

question: Can I cast a spell with a verbal component underwater?
ruling: Reading A: yes. The verbal component rule names a character who is gagged or in an area of silence as unable to cast, and the underwater combat rules limit weapon attacks and grant fire resistance but say nothing about spellcasting. Being underwater is neither named case. Reading B: no. A verbal component is the chanting of mystic words with a specific pitch and resonance; it can't be chanted without speaking, and the text gives no way to speak underwater. Why the text does not settle it: the rule explains what a verbal component is and names two cases that block it, but does not say whether those cases are the only ones, and nothing in the corpus says whether a creature can speak underwater.

question: An enemy shoves me out of its reach. Do I provoke an opportunity attack?
ruling: You don't provoke an opportunity attack when someone or something moves you without using your movement, action, or reaction. A shove is made by the shover, using the Attack action, and pushes the target 5 feet away. Being shoved uses none of your movement, action or reaction, so leaving the enemy's reach this way does not provoke.

question: Can I make an opportunity attack against a creature I can't see?
ruling: You can make an opportunity attack when a hostile creature that you can see moves out of your reach. Seeing the creature is part of the trigger, so a creature you can't see leaving your reach does not give you an opportunity attack.

question: After I Disengage, can I move through an enemy's space?
verdict: no, unless it is at least two sizes larger or smaller than you
ruling: Disengage means your movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks for the rest of the turn; it does nothing else. You can move through a hostile creature's space only if it is at least two sizes larger or smaller than you. Disengaging does not change that, so you can pass through the enemy only if the size rule already allows it.

question: Does moving through an ally's space count as difficult terrain?
ruling: The space of another creature, whether hostile or not, counts as difficult terrain, and every foot of movement in difficult terrain costs 1 extra foot. An ally is a creature that is not hostile, so moving through its space costs double.

question: Can I move between my attacks?
verdict: yes, if your action makes more than one weapon attack
ruling: You can break up your movement on your turn, using some before and some after your action. If you take an action that includes more than one weapon attack, you can also move between those attacks. So you can move between attacks when one action gives you two or more weapon attacks, such as the Attack action with Extra Attack; with a single attack there is nothing to move between, but you can still move before and after it.

question: My Readied trigger and an opportunity attack both happen in one round. Do I get both?
ruling: A readied action is taken with your reaction, and an opportunity attack uses your reaction. When you take a reaction, you can't take another until the start of your next turn. Both need your one reaction, so you get whichever you take first and must give up the other.

question: One member of my party spots the ambush. Is the whole party still surprised?
verdict: no, only those who didn't notice
ruling: Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter, and a member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't. Surprise is decided per creature, so the member who spotted the ambush is not surprised, and each member who didn't notice it is.

question: A flying creature is knocked prone. What happens?
verdict: it falls, unless it can hover or is held aloft by magic
ruling: If a flying creature is knocked prone, it falls, unless it has the ability to hover or is held aloft by magic, such as the fly spell. At the end of a fall a creature takes 1d6 bludgeoning damage for every 10 feet it fell, to a maximum of 20d6, and lands prone. A flier that can't hover and isn't held up by magic falls and takes that damage.

question: Do half cover and three-quarters cover stack?
ruling: If a target is behind multiple sources of cover, only the most protective degree of cover applies; the degrees aren't added together. For example, if a target is behind a creature that gives half cover and a tree trunk that gives three-quarters cover, the target has three-quarters cover. Half cover and three-quarters cover do not stack: only the three-quarters cover applies, a +5 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws.

question: I'm resistant and vulnerable to the same damage type. What happens?
ruling: Resistance halves damage of its type and vulnerability doubles it, and resistance and then vulnerability are applied after all other modifiers to damage. The rule orders the two rather than cancelling them, so the damage is halved and then doubled.

question: Do temporary hit points stack, and do they keep me conscious at 0 hit points?
ruling: Temporary hit points can't be added together: if you have some and receive more, you keep either the old or the new, not the sum. If you have 0 hit points, receiving temporary hit points doesn't restore you to consciousness or stabilize you, though they still absorb damage. So they don't stack, and they don't keep or bring you back to consciousness at 0 hit points.

question: I'm poisoned by two sources. Is it worse than one?
ruling: A poisoned creature has disadvantage on attack rolls and ability checks; that is the whole condition. If multiple situations impose disadvantage on a roll, you still roll only one additional d20. Two sources of the poisoned condition give the same disadvantage twice, which is still one disadvantage, so being poisoned twice is no worse than once.

question: My temporary hit points absorb all of a hit's damage. Do I make a concentration save?
ruling: Reading A: yes. Whenever you take damage while concentrating, you make a Constitution saving throw, and the temporary hit point rule itself says that when you have temporary hit points and take damage, they are lost first. Damage absorbed by them is still damage taken, so the save is made, at DC 10 or half the damage, whichever is higher. Reading B: no. Temporary hit points are a buffer against damage, a pool that protects you from injury; if the buffer absorbs all of it, nothing reaches you, and there is nothing to break your focus. Why the text does not settle it: concentration turns on taking damage, and the text does not say whether damage stopped by temporary hit points counts as taken, beyond the temporary hit point rule's own phrasing.

question: One spell hits me with three separate bolts at once. How many concentration saves do I make?
ruling: Reading A: one. You make a separate saving throw for each source of damage, and the example sources, an arrow and a dragon's breath, are different attackers. One spell is one source, so its bolts call for one save, against the total damage. Reading B: three. Each bolt hits and deals its own damage, as separate attacks do, and each instance of damage is something you take while concentrating, so each calls for a save. Why the text does not settle it: source of damage is not defined, so the text does not say whether it means the spell or each separate hit the spell makes.

question: Can I grapple a creature as my opportunity attack?
ruling: Reading A: yes. An opportunity attack is one melee attack made with your reaction, and a grapple is a special melee attack. A grapple fits the description of the attack the reaction allows. Reading B: no. The grapple rule says you use the Attack action to make it, and a grapple uses a contested check instead of an attack roll; an opportunity attack is a reaction, not the Attack action, so the grapple is not available. Why the text does not settle it: the grapple is called a melee attack but is tied to the Attack action, and the text does not say whether that tie is a requirement or a description of the usual case.

question: A one-minute fight breaks out during a long rest. Do we have to start the rest over?
ruling: Reading A: no. A long rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity, at least 1 hour of walking, fighting, casting spells, or similar adventuring activity. The hour applies to the whole list, so a one-minute fight is far short of it and the rest continues. Reading B: yes. Fighting is not the light activity a long rest allows, which is sleeping, reading, talking, eating or standing watch; and a fight is rarely an hour long, so reading the hour onto fighting would mean fighting almost never interrupts a rest, which suggests the hour binds walking and fighting interrupts outright. Why the text does not settle it: the rule puts one duration in front of a list and does not say whether it applies to each item, and fighting is outside the allowed activities either way.

question: Can I make my two-weapon fighting bonus attack before the attack from my Attack action?
ruling: Reading A: no. When you take the Attack action and attack with a light melee weapon, you can use a bonus action to attack with the other. The bonus attack is granted by that attack, so the attack has to happen first; until it does, you have no bonus action to take. Reading B: yes. You choose when to take a bonus action during your turn unless its timing is specified, and the rule names a condition for the turn, taking the Attack action and attacking with a light weapon, rather than an order. Why the text does not settle it: the word when can be read as a trigger that must come first or as a condition on the turn, and the bonus action rule leaves timing open unless it is specified.

question: I Ready the Attack action and have Extra Attack. Do I make all my attacks when the trigger comes?
verdict: one attack, unless the trigger comes on your own turn
ruling: A readied action is taken with your reaction when its trigger occurs, and a reaction can come on your turn or on someone else's. The Attack action makes one attack, and features can add more; Extra Attack lets you attack twice whenever you take the Attack action on your turn. A readied Attack taken on another creature's turn is not taken on your turn, so it makes one attack. Only if the trigger came during your own turn would Extra Attack apply.

question: I can see an invisible creature with truesight. Do I still have disadvantage attacking it?
ruling: As written, yes: the invisible condition says attack rolls against the creature have disadvantage, with no exception for an attacker who can see it. As intended, no. The condition opens by saying an invisible creature is impossible to see without magic or a special sense, and its penalties follow from that; the unseen attackers rules give disadvantage for attacking a target you can't see. Truesight lets a creature see invisible creatures, so for that attacker the reason for the penalty is gone. The rule as written penalizes an attacker who sees the target clearly, which the rule's own premise does not support, so the intended answer is that the attack has no disadvantage from invisibility.

question: My character is blinded but has blindsight out to 30 feet. Do I have disadvantage attacking a goblin 10 feet away?
ruling: As written, yes: the blinded condition says the creature's attack rolls have disadvantage, with no exception for a creature with blindsight. As intended, no. The condition's penalties follow from its first line, that a blinded creature can't see, and the unseen attackers rules give disadvantage for attacking a target you can't see. Blindsight lets a creature perceive its surroundings without relying on sight within its radius, so a goblin 10 feet away is perceived and the reason for the penalty is gone. Beyond 30 feet blindsight does nothing, and the disadvantage stands.

question: I'm standing inside the area of my own fireball. Can I choose to leave myself out of it?
ruling: An area spell does not pick its targets; it covers an area so it affects multiple creatures at once, and the only locations it leaves out are ones with no unblocked line from the point of origin. A sphere's area extends from its point of origin, so standing inside it puts you in the area. Fireball's own text settles who is caught: each creature in its 20-foot-radius sphere must make a Dexterity saving throw, and it makes no exception for the caster. The targeting rules confirm the caster is not excluded: if you are in the area of effect of a spell you cast, you can target yourself. So the fireball affects you, and you can't opt out.

question: I used my reaction on the last turn of round 1. In round 2 an enemy acts before me and walks out of my reach. Can I make an opportunity attack?
ruling: As written, the text disagrees with itself. The Ready action says you can take only one reaction per round, and round 2 is a new round, so that line allows it. The reactions rule says that when you take a reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn, and your next turn has not started. As intended, no: the reactions rule is the one that defines when a reaction returns, and the Ready line compresses it into a reminder. Your reaction comes back when your turn in round 2 starts, after the enemy has moved.

question: An attack hits me and I cast Shield. Does the +5 AC count against that attack?
ruling: Shield gives a +5 bonus to AC until the start of your next turn, including against the triggering attack. Its casting time is a reaction taken when you are hit by an attack, so it is cast once the hit is known. An attack hits when its total equals or exceeds your AC, so the attack that triggered the spell is checked against your new AC, and one that would have hit by less than 5 misses.

question: An enemy casts Cure Wounds with a 5th-level slot. Does my 3rd-level Counterspell stop it automatically?
ruling: A spell cast with a higher-level slot assumes that slot's level for that casting, so this Cure Wounds is a 5th-level spell. Counterspell stops a spell of 3rd level or lower automatically; against one of 4th level or higher, you make an ability check using your spellcasting ability, DC 10 + the spell's level. So it is not automatic: you need a DC 15 check.

question: My concentration on Haste breaks. What happens to the hasted ally?
verdict: it can't move or take actions until after its next turn
ruling: Haste requires concentration, and a spell that needs concentration ends when concentration is lost. When Haste ends, the target can't move or take actions until after its next turn, as a wave of lethargy sweeps over it. Losing concentration ends the spell like any other ending, so the ally loses the doubled speed, the AC bonus, the advantage on Dexterity saves and the extra action, and then suffers the lethargy.

question: Can I cast Detect Magic without spending a spell slot?
verdict: yes: as a ritual with a ritual-casting feature, or at will with the Eldritch Sight invocation
ruling: Detect Magic has the ritual tag. A spell with that tag can be cast as a ritual, which takes 10 minutes longer than its normal casting time and doesn't expend a spell slot. Casting a ritual requires a feature that grants the ability, and the spell must be prepared or known unless the feature says otherwise. So with such a feature, Detect Magic takes 10 minutes and an action, and costs no slot. A warlock has a second way: the Eldritch Sight invocation lets you cast Detect Magic at will without expending a spell slot. The bard, cleric, druid and wizard each have Ritual Casting: a bard casts as a ritual a spell it knows, a cleric or druid one it has prepared, and a wizard one in its spellbook, prepared or not. The warlock's Book of Ancient Secrets invocation grants ritual casting too.

question: Do temporary hit points count toward Sleep's hit point total?
ruling: Sleep affects creatures in ascending order of their current hit points, and a creature is affected only if its hit points are equal to or less than the remaining total. Temporary hit points aren't actual hit points; they are a separate buffer against damage. So a creature's temporary hit points are not added to its current hit points when Sleep is resolved.

question: I'm invisible from the Invisibility spell and shove someone. Does the spell end?
ruling: Invisibility ends for a target that attacks or casts a spell. A shove is a special melee attack made with the Attack action, using an Athletics check in place of the attack roll. It is still an attack, so shoving ends the spell.

question: My speed is 30 and I'm hasted. I Dash with my action and with Haste's action. How far can I move?
ruling: Haste doubles your speed, so it is 60 feet, and its additional action can be used to Dash. Dash gives extra movement equal to your speed after applying any modifiers, so each Dash adds 60 feet. Your 60 feet of speed plus two Dashes of 60 feet each is 180 feet this turn.

question: When Haste ends, can my ally still take a reaction before its next turn?
ruling: Reading A: no. When Haste ends, the target can't move or take actions until after its next turn, and the reactions rule names a reaction a special action. A reaction is an action of a special kind, so the lethargy forbids it. Reading B: yes. The lethargy forbids exactly the pair the turn rule gives, moving up to your speed and taking one action, and a reaction is a response to a trigger on anyone's turn, limited by its own rule rather than counted among the actions you take on your turn. Why the text does not settle it: Haste does not say whether "actions" includes reactions, and the reactions rule calls a reaction an action while the turn rule treats the action and the reaction as separate things.

question: I attack while invisible from the Invisibility spell. Does that attack get advantage?
ruling: Reading A: yes. The spell ends for a target that attacks, so the attack is what ends it, and the attack is made while the creature is still invisible; an invisible creature's attack rolls have advantage, and a creature that can't see you gives you advantage. Hiding works the same way, giving away your location only when the attack hits or misses. Reading B: no. The spell ends for a target that attacks, and the attack has begun when the roll is made, so the creature is no longer invisible for it; the hiding rule states its timing outright, and Invisibility states none. Why the text does not settle it: the spell names attacking as what ends it without saying whether it ends before or after the attack roll.

question: A creature is 15 feet from my fireball's center but around a corner, with no straight line to it. Is it caught?
ruling: As written, two passages conflict. The area rule says a spell's effect expands in straight lines from its point of origin, and a location with no unblocked straight line to that point isn't in the area. Fireball's own text says the fire spreads around corners. Nothing in this corpus says which governs, and read alone, the area rule leaves the creature out. As intended, Fireball's sentence is the exception it means to make, since it would do nothing if the general rule still held. So the creature, within the 20-foot radius, is caught and must make the saving throw.

question: I can attack twice when I take the Attack action. Can I throw two nets?
ruling: When you use an action, bonus action, or reaction to attack with a net, you can make only one attack, regardless of the number of attacks you can normally make. So an Attack action that throws a net makes one attack, and the second net has to wait for another action. Whatever grants the second attack, the ruling rests on the net's own text.

question: I hit a Large creature with a net. What does it suffer, and how does it get free?
verdict: it is restrained until freed, by a DC 10 Strength check as an action or 5 slashing damage to the net
ruling: A Large or smaller creature hit by a net is restrained until it is freed. Restrained, its speed is 0, attack rolls against it have advantage, its own attack rolls have disadvantage, and it has disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws. It, or another creature within reach of it, can use an action to make a DC 10 Strength check, freeing it on a success. Dealing 5 slashing damage to the net, which has AC 10, also frees it without harming it and destroys the net.

question: I throw a net at an enemy standing right next to me. Do I have disadvantage?
verdict: yes, if the enemy can see you and isn't incapacitated
ruling: A net is a ranged weapon, so throwing it is a ranged attack. You have disadvantage on a ranged attack roll when you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature who can see you and isn't incapacitated. The target being next to you is enough. Its normal range of 5 feet covers the target, so range adds no disadvantage of its own.

question: Can I wield a lance in one hand?
ruling: A lance requires two hands to wield when you aren't mounted. While you are mounted it has no such requirement, so you can wield it in one hand; on foot you need both.

question: Mounted with a lance, I attack one enemy 5 feet away and another 10 feet away. Which attack has disadvantage?
verdict: only the attack on the enemy 5 feet away
ruling: The lance has the reach property, which adds 5 feet to your reach when you attack with it, so the enemy 10 feet away is within reach. You have disadvantage when you use a lance to attack a target within 5 feet of you, and being mounted does not lift it. So the attack on the enemy 5 feet away has disadvantage, and the attack on the one 10 feet away does not.

question: I hold a rapier in one hand and a dagger in the other. Can I use two-weapon fighting?
ruling: Two-weapon fighting lets you use a bonus action to attack with a light melee weapon in your other hand when you take the Attack action and attack with a light melee weapon held in one hand. Both weapons have to be light. The dagger is light, but the rapier's only property is finesse, so the pairing does not qualify, whichever weapon attacks first.

question: With a handaxe in each hand, I attack with one. Can my bonus attack be a throw with the other?
ruling: The handaxe is light, so a handaxe in each hand qualifies for two-weapon fighting: after attacking with one, you can use a bonus action to attack with the other. If either weapon has the thrown property, you can throw it instead of making a melee attack, and the handaxe has it. You don't add your ability modifier to the bonus attack's damage unless it is negative.

question: Can I use my Strength instead of my Dexterity when I throw a dart?
ruling: A dart is a ranged weapon, which uses Dexterity for its attack and damage rolls. It also has the finesse property, and a finesse weapon lets you choose your Strength or Dexterity modifier for the attack and damage rolls, the same modifier for both. So you can throw a dart with Strength.

question: My character is Small. Do they attack with a greatsword at disadvantage?
ruling: The greatsword has the heavy property, and Small creatures have disadvantage on attack rolls with heavy weapons. So a Small character attacks with a greatsword at disadvantage.

question: Wearing a breastplate and carrying a shield, do I have disadvantage on Stealth checks?
ruling: A breastplate imposes no disadvantage on Stealth, unlike half plate among the medium armors, and a shield imposes none either. Neither piece gives disadvantage, so the pair does not.

question: I'm carrying a shield and cast the Shield spell. What is my total AC bonus from the two?
ruling: A shield gives +2 to AC, and the Shield spell gives +5 until the start of your next turn. The rule against combining stops only the same spell's effects from adding together; a shield is not a spell, so nothing stops the two bonuses applying together, for +7 in all.

question: I can attack twice when I take the Attack action. Can I hit with my longsword first, then throw a net with the second attack?
ruling: Reading A: no. When you use an action to attack with a net, you can make only one attack, regardless of the number you can normally make. An Attack action that throws the net is such an action, so it makes one attack in all, and having already swung the longsword, there is no attack left for the net. Reading B: yes. The limit attaches to using an action to attack with a net, and an action begun with a longsword was not used to attack with a net; at most, the net's limit caps the net at one attack, leaving the longsword attack before it untouched. Why the text does not settle it: it says when an action is used to attack with a net but not whether an action whose attacks are split between weapons counts, nor whether the one attack is the action's or the net's.

question: I can attack twice when I take the Attack action, and both daggers are sheathed. Can I draw and throw a dagger with each attack?
ruling: Reading A: no. You can interact with one object for free during your move or your action, such as drawing your weapon as part of the attack. Drawing the second dagger is a second interaction, which takes the Use an Object action, so you throw one dagger and the second attack needs a weapon already in hand. Reading B: yes. Drawing the weapon is given as part of the attack itself, and the ammunition property makes drawing a piece of ammunition part of each attack, so drawing a thrown weapon reads the same way, once per attack. Why the text does not settle it: the thrown property says nothing about drawing, unlike ammunition, and the free interaction's example, drawing a weapon as part of an attack, can be read as spending the one interaction or as part of each attack.

question: My rogue has advantage and attacks with a longsword. Do I get Sneak Attack?
ruling: Sneak Attack adds its damage once per turn to a hit with advantage, but the attack must use a finesse or a ranged weapon. A longsword is a melee weapon whose only property is versatile, so it is neither, and advantage does not make up for it.

question: My ally is next to the goblin I shoot with my shortbow, but an orc is standing next to me. Do I get Sneak Attack?
verdict: no, if the orc can see you and isn't incapacitated
ruling: A shortbow is a ranged weapon, so it qualifies for Sneak Attack, and you don't need advantage when another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it, as long as you don't have disadvantage. But a ranged attack has disadvantage when you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature who can see you and isn't incapacitated, as the orc is. With disadvantage, the ally beside the goblin no longer enables Sneak Attack.

question: I used Sneak Attack on my turn. Can I use it again on an opportunity attack before my next turn?
ruling: Sneak Attack is limited to once per turn, not once per round. An opportunity attack is made with your reaction when a hostile creature leaves your reach, which happens on that creature's turn, so it falls on a turn where you haven't used Sneak Attack. If it hits with a finesse weapon and you have advantage, or another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it and you don't have disadvantage, Sneak Attack applies again.

question: My barbarian rages while wearing chain mail. Do they get resistance to slashing damage?
ruling: Rage grants its benefits, resistance to bludgeoning, piercing and slashing damage among them, only if you aren't wearing heavy armor. Chain mail is heavy armor, so a barbarian raging in it gains none of those benefits.

question: I'm concentrating on a spell when I start raging. What happens to the spell?
ruling: If you are able to cast spells, you can't cast them or concentrate on them while raging. A spell that requires concentration ends when you lose concentration on it, so entering a rage ends the spell.

question: On my turn I only shove an enemy while raging. Does my rage end at the end of my turn?
ruling: A rage ends early if your turn ends and you haven't attacked a hostile creature or taken damage since your last turn. A shove is a special melee attack made with the Attack action, so shoving a hostile creature is attacking it, and the rage continues.

question: Can my monk use Martial Arts with a greatclub?
ruling: Monk weapons are shortswords and any simple melee weapons that don't have the two-handed or heavy property. A greatclub is a simple melee weapon, but it has the two-handed property, so it is not a monk weapon, and Martial Arts' benefits don't apply to it.

question: With the Dueling fighting style, I hold a longsword in one hand and a shield in the other. Do I get the +2 damage?
ruling: Dueling gives a +2 bonus to damage rolls when you wield a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons. A shield is armor, not a weapon, so carrying one leaves you wielding the longsword alone, and the bonus applies.

question: My fighter has Great Weapon Fighting. Can I reroll damage dice with a longsword held in both hands?
ruling: Great Weapon Fighting lets you reroll a 1 or 2 on a damage die for an attack with a melee weapon you wield with two hands, and the weapon must have the two-handed or versatile property. A longsword is versatile, so wielded with two hands it qualifies.

question: With the Two-Weapon Fighting style, do I add my ability modifier to my off-hand attack's damage?
ruling: Two-weapon fighting normally leaves the ability modifier off the bonus attack's damage unless it is negative. The Two-Weapon Fighting style lets you add your ability modifier to the damage of the second attack, so with the style you add it.

question: My 5th-level fighter takes the Attack action and uses Action Surge to take it again. How many attacks is that?
ruling: At 5th level a fighter's Extra Attack lets them attack twice whenever they take the Attack action on their turn. Action Surge grants one additional action on your turn, so taking the Attack action with each gives two Attack actions of two attacks each, four in all.

question: Can my rogue use Uncanny Dodge to halve the damage from a Fireball?
verdict: no; Evasion covers it from 7th level
ruling: Uncanny Dodge halves an attack's damage when an attacker you can see hits you with an attack. Fireball makes no attack; each creature in its area makes a Dexterity saving throw. So Uncanny Dodge does not apply. Evasion, from 7th level, does: against an effect that allows a Dexterity save for half damage, you take no damage on a success and half on a failure.

question: While raging, I throw a handaxe using Strength. Do I add my rage damage bonus?
ruling: Reading A: no. Rage's bonus applies when you make a melee weapon attack using Strength, and throwing a weapon makes a ranged attack, so a thrown handaxe is not a melee weapon attack. Reading B: yes. The handaxe is a melee weapon, and the thrown property has you use the same ability you would for a melee attack with it, Strength; an attack made with a melee weapon using Strength is what the bonus names. Why the text does not settle it: melee weapon attack can be read as a melee attack made with a weapon or as an attack made with a melee weapon, and a thrown melee weapon is the case where the two come apart.

question: Can my rogue Sneak Attack with a thrown handaxe?
ruling: Reading A: no. The attack must use a finesse or a ranged weapon. A handaxe is a melee weapon without finesse, and throwing it makes a ranged attack but does not make it a ranged weapon. Reading B: yes. Thrown, the handaxe is used to make a ranged attack, so the attack uses a weapon as a ranged weapon, which is what the requirement is after. Why the text does not settle it: Sneak Attack names the weapon, not the attack, and the thrown property turns a melee weapon's attack into a ranged one without saying whether the weapon's kind changes with it.

question: With the Dueling fighting style, I throw the dagger I'm holding in one hand. Do I add the +2 damage?
ruling: Reading A: yes. Dueling applies when you wield a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, and gives +2 to damage rolls with that weapon. A dagger is a melee weapon held in one hand, and its thrown damage is a damage roll with that weapon. Reading B: no. Once thrown, the dagger has left your hand, so when its damage is rolled you are no longer wielding it, and the thrown attack is a ranged one. Why the text does not settle it: Dueling names what you wield and the damage roll with it, but not whether the wielding must hold when the damage is rolled or only when the attack is made.

question: Can my halfling fight with a greatsword without any penalty?
verdict: no, they attack with it at disadvantage
ruling: A halfling is Small. The greatsword has the heavy property, and Small creatures have disadvantage on attack rolls with heavy weapons. So a halfling can wield a greatsword, but attacks with it at disadvantage.

question: Can my halfling move through the space of a hostile human?
ruling: You can move through a hostile creature's space only if it is at least two sizes larger or smaller than you, and a Medium human is one size larger than a Small halfling, so the general rule says no. Halfling Nimbleness lets a halfling move through the space of any creature of a size larger than its own, hostile or not, so the halfling can. The space is still difficult terrain, and the halfling can't end its move there.

question: Can my halfling grapple a Large creature?
ruling: The target of a grapple must be no more than one size larger than you. A halfling is Small, and Large is two sizes above Small, so a Large creature is too big for a halfling to grapple.

question: My dwarf has darkvision. Can they see inside the area of a Darkness spell?
ruling: Darkvision lets a creature see in darkness as if it were dim light. The Darkness spell's magical darkness is the exception: a creature with darkvision can't see through it. So the dwarf's darkvision does nothing inside the spell's area.

question: With darkvision, do I have disadvantage on Perception checks in a pitch-dark cave?
verdict: yes, on checks that rely on sight, within 60 feet
ruling: Within 60 feet, darkvision lets you see in darkness as if it were dim light, so darkness is only lightly obscured for you. In a lightly obscured area, creatures have disadvantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sight. So in the dark you can see, but your sight-based Perception checks have disadvantage, and beyond 60 feet the darkness is still darkness.

question: Can the Sleep spell knock out my elf?
ruling: Sleep sends creatures into a magical slumber. An elf's Fey Ancestry says magic cannot put it to sleep, so the spell has no effect on the elf, whatever its hit points.

question: My half-orc has 10 maximum hit points and 5 left, and takes 20 damage. Can Relentless Endurance keep them at 1 hit point?
ruling: The damage reduces the half-orc to 0 hit points with 15 remaining, and remaining damage equal to or more than your hit point maximum kills you instantly. Relentless Endurance works only when you are reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, so it can't save a half-orc from instant death.

question: My half-orc rogue scores a critical hit with a rapier and Sneak Attack. Does Savage Attacks let me roll an extra Sneak Attack die?
ruling: Savage Attacks lets you roll one of the weapon's damage dice one more time on a critical hit with a melee weapon attack. The rapier's damage die is a d8; Sneak Attack's dice are the feature's, not the weapon's. So the extra die is a rapier die, not a Sneak Attack die.

question: Can my halfling use Lucky on a death saving throw?
ruling: Lucky lets a halfling reroll a 1 on the d20 for an attack roll, ability check or saving throw. A death saving throw is a special saving throw, so a 1 on it can be rerolled. That matters, since a 1 on a death save counts as two failures.

question: My halfling rolls with advantage and gets a 1 and a 13. Can I use Lucky?
ruling: Lucky lets a halfling reroll a d20 that shows a 1. When you have advantage or disadvantage and something lets you reroll, you can reroll only one of the dice, and you choose which. So the halfling can reroll the 1 and then take the higher of the new roll and the 13.

question: A red dragonborn breathes on a gold dragonborn, who fails the save. How much damage does the gold dragonborn take?
ruling: A red dragonborn's breath deals fire damage, in full on a failed save. A gold dragonborn's ancestry is also tied to fire, and a dragonborn has resistance to the damage type of its ancestry. Resistance halves the damage, so the gold dragonborn takes half of what was rolled.

question: Does Dwarven Resilience make my dwarf immune to being poisoned?
ruling: Dwarven Resilience gives advantage on saving throws against poison and resistance to poison damage. Neither is immunity: a dwarf that fails the save is still poisoned, with disadvantage on attack rolls and ability checks, and takes half of any poison damage.

question: Can my lightfoot halfling hide behind our human fighter?
ruling: You can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly. A lightfoot halfling's Naturally Stealthy lets it attempt to hide even when it is obscured only by a creature at least one size larger, and a Medium human is one size larger than a Small halfling. So the halfling can try to hide behind the fighter, making a Dexterity (Stealth) check as usual.

question: Does my dwarf get advantage on the saving throw against Poison Spray?
ruling: Reading A: yes. Dwarven Resilience gives advantage on saving throws against poison, and Poison Spray is a puff of noxious gas that deals poison damage, so the save against it is a save against poison. Reading B: no. Poison names the poisons, the substances a creature touches, swallows, inhales or is wounded with, and the poisoned condition; Poison Spray is a spell that deals poison damage, and the trait's resistance to poison damage already covers that. Why the text does not settle it: the trait never says what counts as poison, and the spell is both a gas and a damage type.

question: My half-orc monk scores a critical hit with an unarmed strike. Does Savage Attacks add a die?
ruling: Reading A: no. Savage Attacks rolls one of the weapon's damage dice again, and an unarmed strike is not a weapon, so it has no weapon damage dice to roll. Reading B: yes. An unarmed strike is a melee weapon attack, and Martial Arts has the monk roll a die in place of the unarmed strike's normal damage, so the strike has a damage die for Savage Attacks to roll again. Why the text does not settle it: the trait applies to melee weapon attacks, which an unarmed strike is, but rolls the weapon's dice, which an unarmed strike lacks unless Martial Arts' die counts as one.

question: I'm a fighter 5 / ranger 5 with Extra Attack from both classes. How many attacks do I make when I take the Attack action?
ruling: Each class's Extra Attack lets you attack twice instead of once when you take the Attack action. When you gain Extra Attack from more than one class, the features don't add together, and you can't make more than two attacks with it unless the feature says you do, as the fighter's does only from 11th level in that class. A 5th-level fighter's Extra Attack gives two, so you make two attacks.

question: I'm a paladin 4 / sorcerer 3. What spell slots do I have?
ruling: With the Spellcasting feature from both classes, you use the multiclass rules. Your slots come from adding your full levels in the sorcerer class and half your paladin levels, rounded down: 3 + 2 = 5. On the Multiclass Spellcaster table, 5th level gives four 1st-level, three 2nd-level and two 3rd-level slots. You can use the 3rd-level slots only to cast lower-level spells you know or have prepared.

question: I'm a cleric 2 / paladin 3. How many times can I use Channel Divinity between rests?
ruling: Both classes grant Channel Divinity, and each version is used once before a short or long rest. Gaining the feature from a second class gives you that class's effects but no additional use; more uses come only from a class level that explicitly grants them, as the cleric's 6th level does. So you can use it once between rests, choosing any effect from either class.

question: I'm a barbarian 1 who takes a level in monk. Can I switch to the monk's Unarmored Defense, adding Wisdom instead of Constitution?
ruling: If you already have the Unarmored Defense feature, you can't gain it again from another class. You have the barbarian's version, 10 + your Dexterity modifier + your Constitution modifier, which allows a shield; the monk level does not give you the monk's version.

question: My wizard puts on plate armor. Can she still cast spells?
ruling: Anyone can put on armor, but if you wear armor you lack proficiency with, you have disadvantage on any ability check, saving throw or attack roll that involves Strength or Dexterity, and you can't cast spells. The wizard has no armor proficiency, so in plate she can't cast spells.

question: My cleric has Strength 11 and puts on chain mail. What does it cost her?
verdict: 10 feet of speed, disadvantage on Strength and Dexterity rolls, and no spellcasting
ruling: Chain mail is heavy armor with a Strength requirement of 13; armor with a Strength requirement reduces the wearer's speed by 10 feet unless the wearer's Strength meets it, and 11 does not. The cleric is proficient with light and medium armor and shields, not heavy armor, so she also has disadvantage on any ability check, saving throw or attack roll that involves Strength or Dexterity, and she can't cast spells.

question: My dwarf fighter has Strength 10 and wears plate armor. Is her speed reduced?
ruling: Plate armor requires Strength 15, and heavy armor with a Strength requirement reduces the wearer's speed by 10 feet unless the wearer meets it. A dwarf's speed, though, is not reduced by wearing heavy armor, so her speed stays 25 feet. As a fighter she is proficient with all armor, so no other penalty applies.

question: Woken by an ambush, I spend my first turn putting on my breastplate. Do I get its AC this round?
ruling: A breastplate is medium armor, which takes 5 minutes to don. You benefit from the armor's AC only if you take the full time to don it, so a turn spent on it gives you nothing this round.

question: I throw my longsword at a goblin 30 feet away. What damage does it deal, and does the distance matter?
ruling: The longsword has no thrown property. A melee weapon thrown without that property is an improvised weapon and deals 1d4 damage, and an improvised thrown weapon has a normal range of 20 feet and a long range of 60. At 30 feet the goblin is beyond normal range, so the attack roll has disadvantage.

question: The DM gives me inspiration twice before I use it. Do I have two inspirations?
ruling: You either have inspiration or you don't; you can't stockpile multiple inspirations for later use. The second award gives you nothing more. If you already have it, you can give it up to another player character instead.

question: I roll a 6 on an attack. Can I spend inspiration now to get advantage on it?
ruling: Reading A: no. You expend inspiration when you make the roll, and advantage means rolling a second d20 when you make it, so the choice comes before the d20 is rolled. Reading B: yes. The attack roll is still being made until its result is applied, so inspiration can be spent on it once the 6 is seen. Why the text does not settle it: "when you make" the roll can mean before the d20 is rolled or at any point while it is being resolved, and the text does not say whether a roll already seen can still take advantage.

question: With the Grappler feat I pin a creature I'm grappling. Do my attacks against it have advantage?
ruling: Grappler gives you advantage on attack rolls against a creature you are grappling, and pinning it leaves you and the creature both restrained. Attacks against a restrained creature have advantage, but a restrained creature's own attack rolls have disadvantage, and you are restrained too. When a roll has both advantage and disadvantage, you have neither, however many sources there are of each, so you roll one d20.

question: An enemy fails its save against my caltrops. Can it Dash to keep moving this turn?
ruling: A creature that enters the caltrops and fails its DC 15 Dexterity save stops moving this turn and takes 1 piercing damage. Dash gives extra movement for the turn, but the creature has stopped moving, so it can't use it this turn. The damage also reduces its walking speed by 10 feet until it regains at least 1 hit point.

question: I hit a goblin with a flask of oil, and the next round I hit it with Fire Bolt. How much fire damage does it take?
ruling: A creature hit by thrown oil is covered in it, and if it takes any fire damage before the oil dries after 1 minute, it takes an additional 5 fire damage from the burning oil. Fire Bolt deals 1d10 fire damage on a hit, so the goblin takes 1d10 + 5 fire damage.

question: My wizard didn't prepare Detect Magic today, but it's in her spellbook. Can she cast it as a ritual?
ruling: Detect Magic has the ritual tag. A caster needs a feature that grants ritual casting, and must have the spell prepared or known unless the feature says otherwise. The wizard's Ritual Casting does: she can cast a wizard spell as a ritual if it has the ritual tag and is in her spellbook, without having it prepared. The ritual takes 10 minutes longer and expends no slot.

question: My cleric didn't prepare Detect Magic today. Can he still cast it as a ritual?
ruling: Detect Magic has the ritual tag, but the cleric's Ritual Casting lets him cast a cleric spell as a ritual only if it has the ritual tag and he has it prepared. Without Detect Magic prepared, he can't cast it at all, ritual or not.

question: My 3rd-level wizard finds a scroll of Fireball. Can she copy it into her spellbook?
verdict: no, not until she can prepare 3rd-level spells
ruling: A wizard can copy a spell of 1st level or higher into her spellbook only if it is of a spell level she can prepare, and the spells she prepares must be of a level for which she has spell slots. A 3rd-level wizard has 1st- and 2nd-level slots, and Fireball is a 3rd-level spell, so she can't copy it yet.

question: An invisible mage casts a spell 30 feet from me. Can I Counterspell it?
ruling: Counterspell is a reaction you take when you see a creature within 60 feet of you casting a spell. An invisible creature is impossible to see without magic or a special sense, so without one you can't see the mage casting, and the reaction's trigger never happens.

question: My cleric holds a mace and a shield emblazoned with her holy symbol. Can she cast Bless?
ruling: Bless has verbal, somatic and material components. A cleric can use a holy symbol as a spellcasting focus in place of the material component, and bearing it on a shield counts. A somatic component, though, needs free use of at least one hand, and with a mace in one hand and the shield on the other she has none free. She can cast it only after freeing a hand.

question: I'm attuned to three magic items. Can I attune to a cloak of protection as well?
verdict: no, not without ending one first
ruling: A creature can be attuned to no more than three magic items at a time, and any attempt to attune to a fourth fails. The cloak of protection requires attunement, so its bonus waits on it. You must first end your attunement to one of the three, which takes a short rest focused on that item unless it is cursed, and then spend another short rest attuning to the cloak.

question: My high elf fighter knows one wizard cantrip from his race. Can he attune to a wand of fireballs?
ruling: The wand of fireballs requires attunement by a spellcaster. A creature qualifies as a spellcaster if it can cast at least one spell using its traits or features, not using a magic item or the like. The High Elf Cantrip trait gives him a cantrip from the wizard spell list, and a cantrip is a spell, so he qualifies and can attune to the wand.

question: My 13th-level thief has Use Magic Device. Can she attune to a wand of fireballs, which requires a spellcaster?
ruling: Reading A: yes. Use Magic Device lets her ignore all class, race, and level requirements on the use of magic items, and requiring a spellcaster is a requirement of the class kind: the attunement rules set a spellcaster prerequisite beside a class prerequisite, and the rules for casting from items expect a rogue with Use Magic Device to cast spells from them, at a spellcasting ability modifier of +0. Reading B: no. Use Magic Device names three kinds of requirement, and being a spellcaster is none of them: the attunement rules define it apart from class, as a creature that can cast at least one spell using its traits or features, and a thief casts none. Why the text does not settle it: the spellcaster prerequisite is defined by what a creature can do, not by its class, and the feature's list neither names nor excludes it; the item-spell rules show a rogue with the feature casting from an item without saying whether that item required a spellcaster.

question: Can I wear two rings of protection for a +2 bonus to AC?
verdict: no, only one can be attuned
ruling: The ring of protection requires attunement, and a creature can't attune to more than one copy of an item; the attunement rules use two rings of protection as their example. You can wear both rings, but only the attuned one grants its +1, since without attunement a creature gains only an item's nonmagical benefits.

question: I'm attuned to a ring of protection and a cloak of protection. Do their bonuses stack?
ruling: They stack, for +2 to AC and saving throws. The bar on attuning to more than one copy of an item covers copies of the same item, and these are two different items. The rule that the same effect doesn't combine is written for spells: the effects of the same spell cast more than once don't add together. Neither item is a spell, and no rule stops two different items' bonuses from adding.

question: I found one boot of elvenkind; its mate is lost. Do my steps still make no sound?
ruling: Boots come in pairs, and items that come in pairs impart their benefits only if both items of the pair are worn. One boot of elvenkind gives neither the silent steps nor the advantage on Stealth checks.

question: Can I wear a cloak of protection over a cloak of elvenkind?
verdict: only if the GM allows it
ruling: A character can't normally wear more than one cloak. The rule leaves room for exceptions, and layering two cloaks is its own example of one, so it is the GM's call. Without that allowance, only one of the two cloaks can be worn, and only the worn one works.

question: I'm concentrating on a spell when I cast wall of fire from my staff of fire. Do I keep the first spell?
ruling: A spell cast from a magic item uses its normal duration, and the user must concentrate if the spell requires it. Wall of fire does. Casting another spell that requires concentration ends concentration on the first, since you can't concentrate on two spells at once, so the first spell ends. Paying with the staff's charges instead of a spell slot doesn't change that.

question: Can I use a wand of fireballs while I stand inside a silence spell?
ruling: Silence makes casting a spell with a verbal component impossible, and fireball has one. But a spell cast from a magic item requires no components unless the item's description says otherwise, and the wand's doesn't. A command word can't be spoken in silence either, and the wand needs none: you use an action and expend its charges. So the wand works inside the sphere.

question: Can my thief use Fast Hands to fire a wand of magic missiles as a bonus action?
ruling: Fast Hands lets a thief take the Use an Object action as a bonus action. The wand takes an action to use, but an action that activates a magic item isn't a function of that action, which the item rules call Use an Item, and they name Fast Hands as a feature that can't be used to activate one. Firing the wand takes her action.

question: I score a critical hit with my flame tongue while it's ablaze. Do I roll its fire damage twice too?
ruling: While the sword is ablaze, it deals an extra 2d6 fire damage to any target it hits. On a critical hit you roll all of the attack's damage dice twice, and the rule counts other damage dice the attack involves, such as Sneak Attack's. The flame tongue's 2d6 are dice of the attack's damage, so they become 4d6.

question: My flame tongue is a shortsword, and I hold a dagger in my other hand. Can I ignite the sword and make my off-hand attack on the same turn?
ruling: Speaking the flame tongue's command word takes a bonus action, and so does the second weapon's attack in two-weapon fighting. You can take only one bonus action on your turn, so you choose one: ignite the sword or make the off-hand attack. Lit on an earlier turn, the sword stays ablaze until you speak the word again, drop it or sheathe it, and the off-hand attack is then free to take.

question: I attuned to a berserker axe and found out it's cursed. Can I spend a short rest to end the attunement?
ruling: A creature can voluntarily end attunement by spending a short rest focused on the item, unless the item is cursed, and the berserker axe is. Its curse also makes you unwilling to part with it, keeping it within reach, so leaving it more than 100 feet away for a day is out too. Remove curse is the way: it breaks the owner's attunement to a cursed item so the item can be removed or discarded, though the item's curse remains.

question: Remove curse broke my attunement to a berserker axe, but I'm still carrying it. If an orc hits me, can I still go berserk?
ruling: Reading A: no. The axe's curse reaches you through attunement: becoming attuned extends the curse to you, and remove curse ends every curse affecting you and breaks the attunement, so the berserk save, part of the curse, no longer applies. Reading B: yes. Remove curse leaves the item's curse in place, and the berserk paragraph triggers whenever a hostile creature damages you while the axe is in your possession, with no mention of attunement or of your being cursed, so carrying it still risks the save until you put it down. Why the text does not settle it: the curse section says attunement extends the curse to you, but its berserk trigger is written on possession, and remove curse says the item's curse remains without saying what it does to a holder who isn't attuned.

question: Can I use an Arcana check to steer the sphere of annihilation out of the stone-face trap, the way I could control the item?
ruling: An uncontrolled sphere of annihilation can be levitated by a creature within 60 feet that uses an action and succeeds on a DC 25 Intelligence (Arcana) check. The trap's sphere is the exception: a DC 20 Intelligence (Arcana) check reveals that the mouth holds a sphere that can't be controlled or moved, otherwise identical to a normal one. The check identifies it; it can't steer it.

question: My fighter reaches into the stone face's mouth in the sphere of annihilation trap. Does he lose his arm?
ruling: Reading A: no, he takes 4d10 force damage. The trap's sphere is otherwise identical to a normal one, and the item says anything that touches the sphere but isn't wholly engulfed and obliterated by it takes 4d10 force damage; a fighter with one arm inside is not wholly engulfed. Reading B: yes. The trap says any matter that enters the mouth is instantly obliterated, and the item obliterates all matter it passes through; the arm is matter that entered, so it is gone, and the 4d10 is for the creature that touched it. Why the text does not settle it: one sentence obliterates all matter that enters, another gives damage to whatever touches the sphere without being wholly engulfed, and neither says what happens to part of a creature. The SRD has no rule for losing a limb, so a GM who rules yes rules from outside the corpus.

question: Can I attune to a magic item during a long rest instead of a short one?
ruling: Reading A: yes. Attuning takes a short rest, a period of downtime at least 1 hour long, focused on the item; a long rest is extended downtime that allows light activity, so an hour of it spent focused on the item meets the requirement and the long rest goes on. Reading B: no, not as part of the long rest. The attunement rule names a short rest focused on only that item, and a long rest is spent sleeping or on the light activity it lists; an hour of focus inside it is either a short rest of its own, which a long rest does not contain, or not the rest the rule asks for. Why the text does not settle it: the rule asks for a short rest without saying whether one can sit inside a long rest, and the resting rules define both without saying whether a long rest includes a short one.

question: Can my cleric's Turn Undead send a werewolf running?
ruling: Turn Undead affects each undead that can see or hear the cleric within 30 feet. A werewolf's stat block types it a humanoid, in its human form and its wolf form alike, so it is not undead and the turning doesn't touch it.

question: The werewolf has changed into a wolf. Can I still target it with hold person?
ruling: Hold person targets a humanoid. The werewolf's wolf form keeps its type, humanoid, and its Shapechanger trait says its statistics other than its AC are the same in each form, so the wolf is still a humanoid and a valid target.

question: A ghost has possessed my fighter. Can my cleric's Turn Undead still reach it?
ruling: While it possesses a body, the ghost can't be targeted by any attack, spell or other effect except ones that turn undead, so Turn Undead is the exception its stat block names. If the ghost fails its save it is turned, and being turned ends the possession; the ghost reappears in an unoccupied space within 5 feet of the body.

question: Is poison spray any use against a skeleton?
ruling: A skeleton is immune to poison damage, and poison spray deals only poison damage, so even on a failed save it takes none. The monster rules give creatures immunity to damage types beside resistance and vulnerability, but neither they nor the damage rules say what immunity does; taking no damage of the type is its plain meaning, not a rule the SRD writes down.

question: Can I grapple a ghost to keep it from slipping away through the wall?
ruling: The ghost is immune to the grappled condition, so a grapple can't impose it and there is nothing to hold. Its Incorporeal Movement also lets it move through objects as if they were difficult terrain, so the wall is no barrier to it.

question: My 7th-level rogue succeeds on her Dexterity save against an adult red dragon's fire breath. How much damage does she take?
ruling: Fire Breath calls for a DC 21 Dexterity saving throw, with half damage on a success. Evasion turns an effect that allows a Dexterity save for half damage into no damage on a success and half on a failure, and it names a red dragon's fiery breath as its example. On her success she takes no damage.

question: I saved against an adult red dragon's Frightful Presence last round. Can it frighten me again this fight?
ruling: A creature whose saving throw succeeds, or whose fright ends, is immune to the dragon's Frightful Presence for the next 24 hours. Having succeeded, you can't be frightened by this dragon's Frightful Presence again for a day.

question: The adult red dragon failed its save against my hold monster and chose to succeed instead. How many times can it do that?
ruling: Legendary Resistance lets the dragon choose to succeed when it fails a saving throw, and the adult red dragon has it 3/Day. That notation means three uses, regained when the dragon finishes a long rest, so after the third it must take the saves it fails until it has rested.

question: The dragon just used its fire breath. Can it breathe again on its next turn?
verdict: only if its recharge roll comes up 5 or 6
ruling: Fire Breath is Recharge 5-6. At the start of each of the dragon's turns it rolls a d6 and regains the breath on a 5 or 6, so it breathes again next turn only on that roll and otherwise uses its other actions. A short or long rest also recharges it.

question: Can the adult red dragon use its Wing Attack legendary action in the middle of my turn, right after I attack?
ruling: A legendary creature takes its legendary actions outside its turn, but only one option at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn, regaining the spent ones at the start of its own. Wing Attack, costing two, can't interrupt your turn; the dragon waits until your turn ends.

question: My +1 longsword isn't silvered. Can it hurt a werewolf?
ruling: The werewolf is immune to bludgeoning, piercing and slashing damage from nonmagical weapons that aren't silvered. A magical attack is one delivered by a spell, a magic item or another magical source, and a +1 longsword is a magic item, so its damage isn't from a nonmagical weapon and the immunity doesn't apply; silver matters only for a weapon that isn't magical.

question: My 4th-level druid wants to Wild Shape into a giant spider. Can she?
ruling: Wild Shape's druid level sets the beasts a druid can become: at 4th level, a beast of challenge rating 1/2 or lower with no flying speed. The giant spider is a beast with a climbing speed and no flying speed, but its challenge is 1, above her limit. At 8th level the limit rises to challenge 1, and the spider becomes a form she can take.

question: Can a 1st-level sleep spell put an ogre at full health to sleep?
ruling: Sleep rolls 5d8 for the hit points of creatures it can affect, and a creature is affected only if its current hit points are equal to or less than what remains of the total. An ogre at full health has 59 hit points, more than the 40 that 5d8 can roll at most, so a 1st-level casting can't reach it. Each slot level above 1st adds 2d8, and from a 3rd-level slot, 9d8 can roll 59 or more.

question: My fighter is under protection from evil and good. Can the ghost possess him?
ruling: Protection from evil and good guards against undead, among other types, and its target can't be charmed, frightened or possessed by them. The ghost is undead, so its Possession can't take hold of him while the spell lasts.

question: Can a ghost use Incorporeal Movement to end its turn inside my character's space?
ruling: Reading A: no. Incorporeal Movement lets the ghost move through creatures and objects as if they were difficult terrain, but says nothing about where it may stop, and the movement rules say that, friend or enemy, a creature can't willingly end its move in another creature's space. Reading B: yes. The trait sets the cost of ending a turn inside an object, 5 force damage, which shows it expects the ghost to stop inside what it moves through, and a creature is one of those things, so the trait sets the general rule aside. Why the text does not settle it: the trait prices ending a turn inside an object and is silent on a creature, and whether that silence leaves the general rule in place or the trait's reach covers creatures too is not said.

question: My paladin's longsword hit, with Divine Smite, drops a zombie to 0 hit points. Does it get its Undead Fortitude save?
ruling: Reading A: no. Undead Fortitude doesn't apply when the damage is radiant, and Divine Smite's radiant damage is part of the damage that reduced the zombie to 0 hit points, so the exception holds. Reading B: yes. The hit deals slashing damage as well as radiant, and the exception names damage that is radiant, not damage that includes some; with slashing in the total, the damage isn't radiant, and the zombie saves against DC 5 plus the damage taken. Why the text does not settle it: the trait treats the damage as one thing, radiant or not, and does not say what happens when a single hit deals two types.

question: The ghost has already possessed my fighter. If I cast protection from evil and good on him, does the possession end?
ruling: Reading A: no. The spell says a target already possessed by such a creature has advantage on any new saving throw against the effect, and Possession offers no new save: it lasts until the body drops to 0 hit points, the ghost ends it, or the ghost is turned or forced out by an effect like dispel evil and good. Advantage on a save that never comes does nothing, and the spell needs a willing target while the ghost controls the body. Reading B: yes. The target can't be possessed by undead while the spell lasts, and a possession that continues is the target being possessed, so the spell ends it. Why the text does not settle it: the spell's bar on being possessed may stop a new possession or the state of being possessed, and its own line for a target already possessed grants advantage only on saves this possession doesn't offer.

question: I'm under protection from evil and good when a ghost uses Horrifying Visage on me. Can I still be aged?
ruling: Reading A: yes. The spell keeps you from being frightened by the ghost, not from its other effects: you still make the Wisdom save, and the aging follows a save failed by 5 or more, not the fright, so a bad enough roll still ages you 1d4 x 10 years. Reading B: no. The aging is the frightening effect at its worst, the target also aging on the same failed save that frightens it; with the fright barred, the effect has nothing to add the aging to. Why the text does not settle it: the visage makes one save for two results, and the spell bars only one of them by name without saying whether the other still lands.
